{{Short description|Shape designed to roll down some path}}
[[File:rolling_sphericon.gif|thumb|240px|Animation of a rolling sphericon which makes a sinusoidal path.]]
A '''trajectoid''' is a geometric shape designed to trace a predetermined general periodic trajectory on the plane.<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Sobolev | first1=Yaroslav I. | last2=Dong | first2=Ruoyu | last3=Tlusty | first3=Tsvi | last4=Eckmann | first4=Jean-Pierre | last5=Granick | first5=Steve | last6=Grzybowski | first6=Bartosz A. | title=Solid-body trajectoids shaped to roll along desired pathways | journal=Nature | date=2023 | volume=620 | issue=7973 | pages=310–315 | doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06306-y | pmid=37558849 | bibcode=2023Natur.620..310S | url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-023-06306-y | url-access=subscription }}</ref> Unlike more familiar rolling bodies such as [[sphere]]s or [[cylinder]]s, which follow linear or sinusoidal paths, trajectoids can trace even very complex, custom trajectories. The concept extends earlier studies on rolling objects like [[sphericon]]s and [[oloid]]s, introducing much greater diversity in possible rolling paths.

Physicists and mathematicians from the [[Institute for Basic Science]], [[Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology]] and the [[University of Geneva]], developed an algorithm that defines 3D shapes that will roll under gravity along a general periodic trajectory on an inclined plane (or equivalently can be rolled by hand on a horizontal plane).<ref>{{cite journal  | title = Tumbling Downhill Along a Given Curve  | first1 = Jean-Pierre | last1 = Eckmann  | first2 = Yaroslav I. | last2 = Sobolev  | first3 = Tsvi | last3 = Tlusty  | year = 2024  | doi = 10.1090/noti2947    | doi-access = free| volume = 71 | issue = 6 | pages = 740&ndash;747  | journal = Notices of the American Mathematical Society | arxiv = 2406.16336 }}</ref> This algorithm was realized through 3D printing: Trajectoids were produced by printing two halves and a spherical hollow center which would contain a metal sphere for mass. 

The authors conjectured that trajectoids can be generated for any planar periodic trajectory as long as the trajectoid returns to its original orientation after '''two''' or more periods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Matsumoto |first=Elisabetta |last2=Segerman |first2=Henry |date=2023 |title=Shaped to roll along a programmed periodic path |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-02335-9 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=620 |issue=7973 |pages=282–283 |doi=10.1038/d41586-023-02335-9|url-access=subscription }}</ref> This conjecture was later proved as part of a more general theorem that applies to any system governed by the [[rotation]] group [[SO(3)]] or the unitary group [[Special unitary group|SU(2)]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Eckmann |first=Jean-Pierre |last2=Tlusty |first2=Tsvi |date=2025-10-01 |title=Walks in Rotation Spaces Return Home when Doubled and Scaled |url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/xk8y-hycn |journal=Physical Review Letters |language=en |volume=135 |issue=14 |doi=10.1103/xk8y-hycn |issn=0031-9007|url-access=subscription }}</ref> such as spins, qubits and gyroscopes. The theorem states any series of rotations operating on such a physical system (except for a zero-measure set) can be made to return the system to its original state by uniformly scaling and repeating the series '''twice'''. The existence of trajectoids follows from [[Minkowski's theorem]] and the [[Rodrigues' rotation formula|Rodrigues]] formula for the product of rotation matrices.
